articles.title: Gaza, three years on: Preserving the evidence, breaking the cycle of impunity
articles.author: Shawan Jabarin
articles.content: On October 13, 2023, Al-Haq was among the first to warn states to intervene to stop Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. The continuum of decades of dehumanization of Palestinians, a population subjected to refugeehood, denial of return, killings, torture, property appropriations, and pillage – fragmented and subjugated by Israel’s violent settler-colonial apartheid regime – has resulted in an ongoing Nakba, an ongoing colonial erasure, and escalating destruction of the Palestinian people. Israel’s systematic destruction and annihilation of the Gaza Strip since October 7, 2023, has destroyed all semblance of Palestinian life, leaving Gaza in ruins: Palestinian residences, commercial properties, cemeteries, industries, schools, universities, hospitals, mosques, cultural property, roads, landmarks, and infrastructure have been destroyed, leveled to a barren rubble wasteland. Israel has radically altered the territory of Gaza, constructing military roads, corridors, fortifications and earth berms, appropriating over 70% of Palestinian territory within the so-called Yellow Line , an ever-expanding demarcation line that the Israel forces have claimed as a “new border” in their de facto annexation. Israel imposes a shoot-to-kill policy to prevent Palestinians from returning to their destroyed homes and properties within the Yellow Line, with members of Israel’s security cabinet urging the indiscriminate killing of those approaching the Yellow Line, even “children”. Israeli government plans continue for the construction of Israeli settlements in Gaza and the mass forced transfer of the entire population of Gaza out of the territory, euphemistically termed ‘voluntary emigration’. Over 1.9 million Palestinians in Gaza have been displaced and live in makeshift tents, condensed into encampments in Al-Mawasi, along the seashore, and under the eaves of ruined tower-blocks, denied basic infrastructure necessary for human survival. Despite a so-called ceasefire and the institution of the so-called Board of Peace, Israel has continued to deny the entry of lifesaving reconstruction and humanitarian aid at scale into Gaza. Instead, Palestinians are exposed to the dangers of collapsed buildings, and the entire territory is littered with unexploded ordnance – in Gaza “one person is killed or injured by explosive ordnance each day… nearly half of the victims being children.” Israel continues to carry out lethal attacks, including on Palestinians in tents in humanitarian zones, bringing the total fatalities since the so-called ceasefire of October 2025 to 1,445 Palestinians killed and 5,072 Palestinians injured, while 74,228 Palestinians have been killed and 175,118 Palestinians injured in Gaza since October 7, 2023 – acts which the UN Commission of Inquiry has determined to be genocide. It is impossible for forensic teams and investigators to enter Gaza to investigate the genocide and international crimes. Israel controls all access points into Gaza, including the Rafah Crossing, defying the International Court of Justice (ICJ) Provisional Measures Orders in South Africa v. Israel , to end all military operations in Rafah. Israel’s continued military presence as occupying power in Gaza further breaches an ICJ Advisory Opinion from July 2024, requiring that Israel immediately withdraw its unlawful military presence from the Palestinian territory. Evidence collection is severely hampered under the ongoing blockade that defies the orders of the International Court of Justice. Israel is unlawfully occupying the entire Palestinian territory, including Gaza, and is continuing to breach the orders of the ICJ by failing to ‘take effective measures to prevent the destruction and ensure the preservation of evidence related to allegations of acts within the scope of Article II and Article III of the [Genocide] Convention’. This includes taking effective measures ‘to ensure the unimpeded access to the Gaza Strip of any commission of inquiry, fact-finding mission or other investigative body mandated by competent organs of the United Nations to investigate allegations of genocide’. To block the collection of evidence, Israel has targeted journalists in a pattern of attacks, killing at least 260 journalists since October 2023, erasing the documentation of its crimes in Gaza, while smearing the deceased with fabricated accusations of militant involvement. Only military embeds chaperoned and censored by the IOF are granted access to Gaza. As UN Special Rapporteur Irene Khan reports, “Gaza has become the deadliest conflict ever for journalists.” Israel’s killings and international crimes in Gaza are self-investigated by Israel’s Military Advocate General, who systematically shields the Israeli military from punishments, including by dropping charges against five Israeli soldiers filmed gang-raping a Palestinian detainee – the details of which informed the UN Secretary General’s reported decision to include Israel among the countries blacklisted on the conflict-related sexual violence register. Al-Haq’s engagement has used accountability to force states and companies to curtail their supply of armaments to Israel and to recognize that genocide is taking place in Gaza as defined by international conventions. Within this context, for human rights organisations, such as Al-Haq, whose work supports ongoing criminal investigations at the International Criminal Court, presence in Gaza is more crucial than ever. Al-Haq monitors and documents violations, investigating patterns of attacks, with an expanded field team that takes testimonies and collects documentation on the ground in Gaza. This includes the testimonies of Palestinian detainees released from Israel’s torture prison Sde Teiman and other detention camps. This documentation has been used in submissions to the UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territory to inform her report on Torture, and the UN Committee Against Torture, who found a ‘troubling… State policy of organized and widespread torture and ill-treatment’. Al-Haq has always engaged to preserve the evidence of Palestinian erasure and the documentation of Israel’s settler colonial crimes. Its paper records date back to 1979, and the institution is in the process of digitising this massive record for posterity. Today, its work continues both within and outside Palestine. The team is collecting testimonies from Palestinians who have left Gaza, those who managed to escape to Egypt prior to the attacks on Rafah in April 2024, and medics who have borne witness to the genocide in hospitals and health facilities. To adapt to the conditions of denied entry and the scale and magnitude of the destruction of Gaza, Al-Haq’s Forensic Architecture Unit compiles digital investigations, reconstructing the attacks on Al-Tabaeen school, and the Indonesian Hospital, using open-source information and satellite imagery, mapping, and 3D modelling and drawing from a large databank of carefully collected video and open-source evidence, along with a registry of genocidal statements. In the last three years, Al-Haq has prioritized accountability, entering partnerships and coalitions with civil society organisations in third states. The aim is to pursue individual, corporate, and state perpetrators of international crimes and international wrongful acts that contribute to the maintenance of Israel’s genocidal settler-colonial apartheid regime in denial of the inalienable rights of self-determination and return for Palestinians. Since October 7, 2023, Al-Haq has taken on more than 30 cases in 13 jurisdictions. These include arms cases against Australia, Canada, Denmark, France, the Netherlands, Poland, Germany, the UK, and the United States. While a number of these cases were deferred back to national governments pending separation of powers restrictions, there have also been very significant victories in Australia, Canada, and the UK, resulting in the disclosure of important state documentation that details the extent of the arms export trade. Combined litigation and advocacy pressures have also resulted in the curtailment of arms exports from Canada, the Netherlands, and the UK to Israel that are in breach of international humanitarian law. Further, cases in the United States and the Netherlands have resulted in important recognitions of plausible genocide and genocide taking place in Gaza. While these cases are mostly judicial reviews to halt the supply of arms to Israel, they are important emergency actions that should be seen as a pressure point, along with advocacy and campaigning to force state action. Al-Haq, along with partners in Australia, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, and Switzerland, has also pursued individuals that include Israel’s President Herzog and Israel’s Minister of Economy Nir Barkat for international crimes, with Israel’s Minister of Finance Bezalel Smotrich cancelling his planned trip to France following Al-Haq’s submission of a case file to the War Crimes Unit there. Coordinating with partners and war crimes units in Belgium, France, Germany, and Italy, Al-Haq has submitted files of evidence against dual Israeli nationals for their part as snipers in Israel’s Ghost Unit in Gaza, killing Palestinians in genocidal attacks. The Dutch company “The Four Winds”, which supplies attack dogs to the Israeli forces that used these in the brutalization, torture, and rape of Palestinian detainees, announced its ceasing of activities following Al-Haq’s joint legal action in the Netherlands. In France, the Paris Judicial Court issued a summons against French Israeli dual national Nili Kupfer-Naouri, president of the Zionist settler organization “Israel Is Forever”, for complicity in genocide. We will continue to relentlessly pursue the perpetrators of atrocities in Gaza and against the Palestinian people. These cases are just a drop in the ocean. Given the scale of the killings, and other genocidal acts and the clear state intent to destroy the Palestinian people, the severity and magnitude of these crimes requires recourse to the international courts: the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice. Al-Haq, Al Mezan, and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights have engaged the ICC since the first preliminary examination in 2009, and since 2015 have submitted and continue to submit files of evidence to the prosecutor, for investigation into the Situation in Palestine. On November 21, 2024, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israel’s Prime Minister Netanyahu and former Minister of Defense Gallant for international crimes against Palestinians in Gaza, including the crime against humanity of murder. There may be many more applications for arrest warrants against senior Israeli politicians and military leaders before the court. However, following a decision of the court in April 2025, to no longer publish the prosecutors’ requests in the Situation in Palestine, this information is no longer public – with serious consequences for deterrence. The prosecutor has since been removed by the Assembly of States Parties in disciplinary proceedings directly exploited by Israel in a targeted smear campaign, leaving the court fragile and vulnerable to political interference and attack. In September 2025, the US sanctioned Al-Haq, Al Mezan, and PCHR for their work in supporting the ICC, along with its sanctioning of ICC judges, prosecutors, and the UN Special Rapporteur on the oPT. The United States has further sanctioned Palestinian prisoners’ rights NGO Addameer, along with representatives of the PLO and PA, to crush international accountability work on Palestine, cripple Palestinian institutions, and destroy the International Criminal Court. Despite these attempts, our work perseveres, and the arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant remain active. Beyond criminal proceedings, the International Court of Justice holds the key to addressing root causes. Already, the ICJ has ruled on ending Israel’s presence in the oPT, finding Israel’s occupation in breach of peremptory norms of international law. The Nicaragua v. Germany case is possibly the most important case currently pertaining to state responsibility before the ICJ. The case concerns Germany’s responsibility for supplying arms to maintain Israel’s unlawful presence and apartheid in Palestine, and Germany’s complicity and failure to prevent acts of genocide in Gaza. Should the case proceed to the Merits, it will have a deep imprint on regulating and constraining the acts of all Third States in Palestine. Finally, although not until 2031, the ICJ will hear the Merits in South Africa v. Israel , one of the most important cases to ever come before the ICJ, with the possibility of awarding restitution and reparations to South Africa for the benefit of the Palestinian people and cementing for the historical record Israel’s responsibility for the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza. Shawan Jabarin is the general director of Al-Haq. He was Amnesty International’s first Palestinian Prisoner of Conscience, having been held in an Israeli prison for eight years over a number of years. He has worked for years promoting human rights in the face of Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territory. This article was produced by Globetrotter .

articles.title: Iran calls for the end of the war after Trump admits it led to defeat in midterm elections
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: After US President Donald Trump reiterated that his party lost the midterm elections because of the US-Israeli war on Iran, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi asked him to respect the wishes of the American people and end the war now. “They did not like the war. They did not like the fact that gasoline went up, ‘cause I had it down at a low, there’s-a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel,” Trump said during a 60 Minutes interview on Sunday, while underlining reasons why Republicans lost the November 3 midterm elections. Though Trump did not directly blame Israel for the war, Araghchi pointed out that people’s disgust with Israel is rooted in the fact that it has been largely seen as the reason behind the war. Trump “clearly recognizes that the vast majority of Americans are disgusted with Israel” which has bamboozled successive “US administrations into forever wars,” Araghchi said in a post on X on Monday, November 9. Earlier, US Vice President JD Vance had also blamed relations with Israel for the war on Iran, claiming it caused unpopularity for the Republican party in the elections and called for changes to those relations. Araghchi affirmed there should be no further delays and the war should end as both the people in the US and the people of West Asia have seen and suffered enough. Replying to a related question about the possibility of restarting the war, Trump contradicted his own statements made earlier on Wednesday and Thursday, claiming he is not looking to escalate the war as there is no reason for it now. He further said that Iran’s nuclear program is practically over as they do not have any nuclear material left, and he “has stopped them from having a nuclear weapon.” Trump claimed that though there is no need to strike Iran now, if such a need arises in the future, for example to attack Pickaxe Mountain (an alleged Iranian nuclear site) “we would have that done in one hour.” Strait of Hormuz When asked about the cost of the war and the deployment of US assets to protect navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, Trump claimed that the Strait was open. He also claimed that all its allies in the region, including Israel, would not have survived without the US support and therefore they are going to pay for all the costs the US has incurred in the war and managing the traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has repeatedly denied US claims about the Strait being open. It has targeted dozens of ships trying to cross the Strait with the US help and claimed only ships coordinating with Iran are allowed to cross it. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced additional measures to control what it called the “smuggling” of oil through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, claiming to have destroyed the “enemy’s” navigation aid systems. In an earlier post on Sunday , Araghchi had reiterated the Iranian proposal to open the Strait. He has said that if the US agrees to its demands the waterway would open in two days, asking the White House to learn from the American people and make its choice. Araghchi had proposed last month that if the US agrees to its seven demands, including the end of the war on all fronts in the region, the lifting of all sanctions imposed since the collapse of the June 17 Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), and releases its frozen assets, Iran will move to open the Strait of Hormuz within days. The US has rejected the Iranian demands to end the war and open the Strait of Hormuz. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called them “outrageous and ridiculous.” Responding to Rubio’s rejection, Esmail Baghaei, official spokesperson of Iran’s Foreign Ministry questioned his reasoning on Monday, claiming if anything was really outrageous and ridiculous it was the US-Israeli war on Iran. US aggressive posture against Iran continue The US has repeatedly quoted data to prove the “normalization” of the energy trade through the Strait of Hormuz, with Trump making claims that the US is in full control of the waterways. The US Central Command has continued to make aggressive postures. On Friday, it launched fresh airstrikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island. Though Iran claimed the strike failed to cause any substantial damage. On Sunday the US also announced the formation of a 20-member so-called “Iron Gate” task force in an effort to prevent the transportation of weapons and other goods through Iranian borders, as an extension of its naval blockade. One of the objectives of the task force is to also prevent trade by land and the Caspian sea routes as a part of the US attempts to “economically isolate” Iran. Over the weekend, the US Department of State also launched a so-called Rewards for Justice campaign, announcing a $20 million reward and “possible relocation” for “information about Iran’s nuclear program including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community.” Iran reacted sharply to the move, calling it a “bid to recruit accomplices for assassinations, criminal acts and further offensive.” Adding to the confusion on Sunday, Trump also claimed that he is going to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping during the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China next week, where they will be discussing the future of denuclearization and the “end of the war” on Iran. Both Russia and China have been demanding the end of the US-Israeli war on Iran, with Russia even offering mediation.

articles.title: Garment workers in Bangladesh take their struggle for decent wages to the streets
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: For multiple days, thousands of workers in Bangladesh, mostly from garment factories, protested for a raise in their minimum monthly wages and against the rising prices of essential commodities, defying the state’s oppressive measures. On Tuesday, November 3, news reports indicated fresh clashes between workers and security forces at various places in the capital, Dhaka, with the agitating workers trying to block highways and other roads. The protests broke out despite the Home Minister of the country Salahuddin Ahmed warning the workers to return to work on Monday after claiming their demands had been addressed by the government through the formation of a “wage board.” Meanwhile, the authorities unleashed violence and repression on workers with police resorting to baton charges and firing tear gas at various places injuring several of them. The police have also arrested protesters after accusing them of indulging in arson and violence. Workers are demanding a revision in their minimum monthly wages to at least 30,000 Bangladeshi Taka (around $240) from its present 12,500 (around $100) claiming the present wages are highly inadequate to live a decent life in the context of the rising prices of essential commodities, including food and fuel. Several unions and progressive organizations, including the Workers Party of Bangladesh (WPB), however, have demanded an even higher wage of Taka 37,125 (around $300) along with measures to curb the rising prices of essential commodities. The protests began in Dhaka in the last week of October and continued throughout the weekend. After the government failed to respond to their demands, workers blocked several roads in the city including some highways on Saturday and Sunday. Dozens of factories in Gazipur and other industrial areas of Dhaka declared holidays on Monday and Tuesday in an attempt to avoid gatherings. The government has also increased the deployment of security forces at all major points in the city to prevent agitating workers from blocking roads and taking out other militant actions. Decent living wages Workers in Bangladesh argue that the minimum wages in the country have not been revised for years now despite the rise in profits for the companies, higher revenues from garment exports, and rising prices of the essential commodities. Bangladesh is the world’s second largest exporter of garments, after China, with around 80% of all its export value coming from the sector alone. According to various studies , the wages of garment sector workers in Bangladesh remain lowest among all the major exporting countries. Workers in the garment sector are also among the lowest paid workers in the country. Bangladesh has seen a consistent increase in inflation in the last four years which, in the absence of a corresponding rise in wages, has actually led to a drop in the real wages . Just for an example, the official inflation rate in September was over 8%. This has created a severe cost of living crisis for most of the workers in the country. The recent high inflation in the prices of the essential commodities in the country is partially attributed to the ongoing US-Israeli war on Iran and continued disruptions in the transportation of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz. Bangladesh imports nearly half of its oil and gas needs from the Gulf. The US-Israeli aggression and Iranian retaliation has disrupted these imports, leading to severe shortages of cooking gas and oil also affecting the prices of other commodities, including food. The WPB issued a press release on Monday in support of agitating workers and condemning the “brutal suppression by law enforcement agencies and hired thugs” on them. Prothom Alo , a prominent local daily, reported on Tuesday that, along with the security forces, workers of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) were also involved in repressive activities. The WPB also condemned the attempts by certain sections of the ruling establishment and the media to vilify protests by calling them a “conspiracy.” It expressed hope that the BNP-led right-wing government would understand the gravity of the situation and immediately address the demands raised by the workers.

articles.title: India in the Mediterranean
articles.author: Zoe.
articles.content: On October 26, 2026, Greece’s Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis stood at the United Nations headquarters and rejected the maritime agreement between Turkey and Libya. Gerapetritis spoke on behalf of Greece of course, but also Bahrain, Cyprus, Egypt, the European Union, and the United Arab Emirates. Five days later, the Indian frigate INS Trishul entered Souda Bay in Crete as part of activities with the US Navy installation (Naval Support Activity) and with the NATO Maritime Interdiction Operational Training Center. The sequence illuminates a developing strategic geography: India’s naval reach, its confrontation with Pakistan’s new Turkish partner, and its ambition to connect Indian capital to European markets increasingly converge in the eastern Mediterranean. Energy fields On October 20, the Libyan Government of National Accord in Benghazi approved a maritime memorandum signed with Türkiye in 2019. Greece, which has a hostile relationship with Türkiye, argues that the delimitation in the memorandum disregards the maritime entitlements of islands that Greece claims, such as Crete; the European Union (EU), agreeing with Greece, argues that this memorandum infringes the rights of third party states. Of course, Türkiye welcomed the decision from Benghazi and rejected the EU statement. These arguments are weighed down by the oil that lies beneath the waves. In February, Chevron and Helleniq Energy signed an agreement to explore four offshore Greek oil blocks, including two south of Crete. Chevron holds a 70% operating interest in this endeavor, which envisaged seismic exploration of potential fields. The concessions show why maritime boundaries matter, since competing maps can have an enormous impact on future discoveries of oil. Indian Odyssey In August 2023, India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi went to Athens and met with Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis. They signed an agreement that reinforced the India-EU Connectivity Partnership of May 2021, which on the surface covers a great deal of ground but which underneath it is mainly about deals for large corporations around ports, submarine cables, and satellite networks. In February 2024, Modi and Mitsotakis explicitly connected cooperation in the eastern Mediterranean with the US war aims Asia, writing of – in the Greek version – “a free, open, and rules-based Mediterranean Sea and Indo-Pacific” (Modi said to Mitsotakis that “it is a matter of joy that Greece has decided to join the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative”, an Indian-driven platform for scientific cooperation but mainly for maritime security). The institutional relationship has since deepened with a February 2026 Joint Declaration of Intent on defense industrial cooperation and then with a Bilateral Military Cooperation Plan. India’s Defense secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh visited Cyprus and Greece in mid-October to follow-up on the India-EU Security and defense Partnership . As India and Greece struck these diplomatic and military deals, Indian navy vessels came one-by-one to Greece. Before the INS Trishul , the INS Tamal called at Souda Bay in August 2025, while INS Trikand reached Salamis in September 2025 and participated in the first India-Greece naval exercise. Why is Modi’s India so eager for this arrangement with Greece? Apart from the words on the text, two other contextual issues bear mention: first, the commercial arrangements led by Modi’s major corporate backer, Gautam Adani, and second, the emergent arrangements for West Asian security developed by Pakistan, Türkiye, and Saudi Arabia. Adani’s ports In 2022, Gautam Adani’s Adani Ports built a joint venture with the Israeli firm Gadot to acquire Haifa port in Israel, with Adani holding 70%. This acquisition allowed Adani to build a substantial position at a Mediterranean gateway. Less than a year later, in September 2023, at the G20 summit in New Delhi, several countries such as India and the United States joined the European Union to announce the creation of an India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor ( IMEC ). The IMEC process forms part of the US-backed effort to offer an alternative to the Chinese-led Belt and Road Initiative. The pathway is simple: it begins in Gujarat and Maharashtra, goes to the Gulf by ship, connects to railways through Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Israel, then from Israel it moves to Greece and France. What is striking is that across the entire landscape of the IMEC are properties owned by Adani’s various corporations: from the ports at Kandla and Mundra (in Gujarat, India) to Haifa (Israel) and then to Marseille (with the continued attempt to acquire stakes in Greek ports). In a sense, the IMEC is less a network of nations and more a global chain of Adani-owned ports. IMEC’s proposed itinerary deliberately bypasses Türkiye, privileging a Gulf-Israel-Europe connection that serves Washington’s regional integration agenda while limiting Ankara’s role as a transit power. US President Joe Biden explicitly presented it as a contribution to an economically integrated Middle East that made Israel the Mediterranean transit point rather than Türkiye. The logic of this route must be understood in light of the Abraham Accords , which was designed by the United States to push various Arab states to normalize relations with Israel formally. The IMEC, with Saudi Arabia urged to allow trade lines to run through Israel, would have de facto ended up being an exercise in normalization. The necessity to avoid Türkiye and go through Israel was not about commerce but entirely, for the United States, about the politics of normalization for Israel. The Mecca Agreement The US-Israeli attack on Iran changed the entire paradigm of security in West Asia. Iran’s retaliation against US military bases in the Gulf Arab states sent a message that the US cannot be an adequate defense shield for these regions. The general view is now that the countries of West Asia need to come together to seek their security through negotiations. On August 7, 2026, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye signed a joint defense agreement that treated an armed attack on one as an attack against all three. Prior to that announcement, Pakistan’s Asim Munir went to Tehran to inform the Iranian leadership that the Mecca agreement was not designed against Iran but to create a platform that did not include the United States (and by October, defense ministers from all three countries went to Iran to defuse any tensions). On August 11, India’s officials said that they were monitoring the situation, and later in the month when Bangladesh said it was considering membership, India repeated again that it had its eye on the agreement. Little written about in all this is Pakistan’s growing relationship with Türkiye. In February 2025, Ankara and Islamabad signed agreements covering electronic warfare cooperation, military personnel exchanges, and training in military health. Three months later, in May, India and Pakistan conducted an air war in which Pakistan used Türkiye-origin YIHA-III and Asisguard Songar drones (with an additional controversy, denied by Ankara, that six Turkish military aircraft landed in Pakistan in late April). On September 22, 2026, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan raised the matter of Kashmir at the UN General Assembly, which India rejected a week later. India’s cultivation of Greece, which has its own conflicts with Türkiye over Cyprus, offers Delhi potential influence in Türkiye’s neighborhood. Saudi Arabia’s dance between its intimacy with the United States and its eagerness to be a player in its neighborhood means that it was an original IMEC participant in 2023 and an original signatory of the Mecca Agreement in 2026. Officials close to the Saudi palace – reaffirmed by Reuters – say that Mohammed Bin Salman, the titular leader of the country, has been closely assessing the shifts in world power away from the United States and is eager to join or build platforms (such as the BRICS+) that bring Saudi Arabia closer in line with the multilateral system. India’s Mediterranean engagement combines commercial expansion with strategic calculation. But does the entry of India into a conflict between Greece and Türkiye, and into the Israeli occupation and genocide of the Palestinians benefit India’s people or does it do the work of US and NATO foreign policy? Extending the India-Pakistan conflict into the Mediterranean brings one more set of tensions into waters that already have sufficient problems. The profits of a port operator offer an inadequate measure of the national interest. Vijay Prashad is an Indian historian and journalist. He is the author of forty books, including Washington Bullets, Red Star Over the Third World, The Darker Nations: A People’s History of the Third World, The Poorer Nations: A Possible History of the Global South, and How the International Monetary Fund Suffocates Africa, written with Grieve Chelwa. He is the executive director of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research , the chief correspondent for Globetrotter, and an editor at LeftWord Books (New Delhi). He also appeared in the films Shadow World (2016) and Two Meetings (2017). This article was produced by Globetrotter .

articles.title: Trump lost Congress. The US is losing the world | w/ Vijay Prashad
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: Iran is still restricting the Strait of Hormuz, Ukraine’s front lines haven’t moved, and China won’t be contained. Even before voters handed Democrats Congress, Vijay Prashad argues Washington was already losing its grip on the world. The Tricontinental executive director joins Rania Khalek and Zoe Alexandra from Kenya to break down what the 2026 midterms mean for US foreign policy. As Trump admits the Iran war cost Republicans, and JD Vance blames it outright, Prashad says the US is “at a loss strategically,” with Tehran holding the leverage, backed by Russia and China. Prashad is hopeful that new faces like Abdul El-Sayed and six new DSA members, backed by pressure from below, can force “irrelevant” Schumer and Jeffries to answer to the new progressive wing. Khalek pushes back: insurgents will be co-opted, zionist corporate-backed Dems still hold the power, and the fight over leadership matters. They also discuss Palestinian parties holding the balance of power in Israel’s Knesset, Europe’s backlash against militarization and conscription, why Prashad thinks a Democratic Congress is too late to change the war in Ukraine or the drive to war with China, and why Lula’s re-election in Brazil shows Trump “lost the hemisphere.” Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! #breakthroughnews ****** Rough transcript follows: [Interviewer:] Welcome to the show, Vijay Prashad, Executive Director of the Tricontinental Institute for Social Research. [Vijay Prashad:] Thanks for having me. It’s an honor to be your first guest. [Interviewer:] We’re excited to have you. Let’s start with the unpopular war in Iran. We’ve heard from JD Vance, Trump, and polling that indicates people in the US voted against the Iran war. However, Iran doesn’t see this as a change of heart. Khamenei said expecting partisan change to end US hostility is gravely mistaken. Can Trump still prosecute this war after losing Congress? Do his prospects change with a Democrat-controlled Congress, and do they want to end this war? [Vijay Prashad:] Firstly, I was talking to people in Tehran, and they joked that Trump and Netanyahu started a war thinking they’d change the regime in Tehran, but instead, it created regime change in Israel and Washington. Interestingly, on November 2nd, before the election, IRGC head Mohsen Rezaei had a 90-minute phone call with Vladimir Putin. On November 5th, Rezaei flew to Moscow with a message from Ayatollah Khamenei. Russia and China have been in talks, wanting to see hostilities decrease. The US attack on Qeshm Island was minimal, and the US is not strategically capable of further attacks on Iran. Iran holds the cards and demands confidence-building measures, such as ending the embargo on the Strait of Hormuz and releasing frozen assets. The US is at a loss on how to proceed. Democrats coming into Washington, with the increase of Democratic Socialists of America, might bring new voices. If they are more like Rashida Tlaib than Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, they could be interesting voices. Even though it’s the party of Biden, the new representatives might propose legislation to prevent more war and suffering. [Interviewer:] It’s exciting to have people who speak against sanctions and bombing campaigns. However, the Democratic Party was responsible for the initial genocide in Gaza. There hasn’t been accountability, and the leadership remains Zionist and imperialist. Do you see a change in Israel policy, or will it be the same policies glossed over with liberalism? [Vijay Prashad:] Politics doesn’t happen in a straight line. In Israel, a historic number of Palestinians voted, resulting in a high number of Palestinian lawmakers in the Knesset. They now hold the keys, demanding a rollback of apartheid policies. In the US, pressure from below is crucial. Newly elected representatives need to be informed about the implications of foreign policy on domestic issues. The new class should challenge Schumer and Jeffries’ leadership. [Interviewer:] While it’s important to be optimistic, we must remember recent history. Some insurgent candidates might compromise once in power. The Democratic Party is still run by corporate interests, and movement building outside the party remains crucial. [Vijay Prashad:] I agree, but it’s also okay to declare victory. Trump’s defeat is significant, and millions voted against his policies. The focus should be on organizing their thinking and putting pressure on newly elected officials. This wasn’t a victory for Schumer and Jeffries; it’s about the people who voted against Trump’s policies. [Interviewer:] Let’s discuss the war in Ukraine. Democrats support funding the war, and some progressive insurgents are on board. What does a Democratic Congress mean for NATO, and how long will this war continue? [Vijay Prashad:] The new Congress is late to the game. Europe is on fire, with people protesting military spending. No one wants to die in a Ukrainian ditch. The war is over, and the only solution is a conclusive peace settlement. More money to Ukraine won’t change the situation. [Interviewer:] Regarding China, do Democrats represent a break in the drive to war, or will they try to outflank Trump as hawks on China? [Vijay Prashad:] It’s too late. The US establishment acknowledges it’s too late to push China’s development back. China’s economic advancement is the real threat, not military. The US can’t intimidate China, and it must focus on building its own infrastructure. The world is no longer willing to be intimidated. [Interviewer:] Thank you, Vijay Prashad, for joining us. We look forward to discussing more topics with you in the future.

articles.title: “Hatemonger” as Chief of Staff: Trump Taps Stephen Miller to Top Role After Massive Election Defeat
articles.content: Stephen Miller, the architect of the Trump administration’s mass deportation policies, has replaced Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. In a recent 60 Minutes interview, President Donald Trump acknowledged that his immigration policies may be “too tough” and contributed to his party’s steep losses in the midterm elections, but in elevating Miller, he is “choosing to double down,” says journalist Jean Guerrero. “Stephen Miller enables [Trump] in this instinct to choose cruelty over everything else,” she says. Guerrero is a New York Times contributing opinion writer, USC journalism professor and author of Hatemonger: Stephen Miller, Donald Trump, and the White Nationalist Agenda .

articles.title: “Right Now My Vote Is No”: L.A.’s DSA Rep.-Elect Gonzales-Torres on Backing Jeffries for House Speaker
articles.content: The next Congress will include about 100 new lawmakers in the House of Representatives, the largest freshman wave in decades. That also includes six newly elected members of the Democratic Socialists of America, bringing the total number of DSA members in Congress to eight. One of the incoming DSA congressmembers will be California’s Angela Gonzales-Torres, who worked two other jobs while campaigning and was massively outspent by her opponent, incumbent Democratic Congressmember Jimmy Gomez. In her first national TV interview, Gonzales-Torres tells Democracy Now! she will prioritize immigrant justice, Medicare for All and fighting corruption, when she is sworn in. She also explains why she has not yet committed to supporting Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker. “As of right now, my vote is no,” she says. “Over 100,000 Angelenos voted for courage. They voted for change.”

articles.title: “A Crackdown on All Independent Voices”: Egypt Shutters News Outlets, Prosecutes Editor Lina Attalah
articles.content: Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr , faces a criminal trial this week on charges of “spreading false information,” just two weeks after being convicted of operating an unlicensed website and fined more than $50,000. A judge also ordered the publication to be shut down. The cases are part of a broader crackdown on independent Egyptian media under the government of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, including the arrest of the entire newsroom of another outlet, _ Matsadaash_. More than 100 organizations, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, have condemned the arrests and prosecutions and called on Egyptian authorities to drop the charges. “Putting us in jail is not going to solve the country’s problems,” Attalah told Democracy Now! in an interview Friday. “We need to be operating as journalists in our newsrooms as opposed to being defendants in courtrooms.” Attalah says she and Mada Masr will appeal the ruling to shut them down, hoping to “use this crisis” as a way to fight censorship in Egypt and expand the space for independent reporting.

articles.title: Are Mexican cartels using Ukraine’s war as a training ground for drone warfare?
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: Several weeks ago, videos posted on social media allegedly showed Mexican mercenaries in Ukraine who claimed to belong to powerful Mexican cartels. Those appearing in the videos are wearing the uniform of the Ukrainian army, which is currently engaged in a war of attrition against Russia. A video released by Al Jazeera shows an unidentified person claiming to be part of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), and another who says he is part of “La Chapiza,” a faction led by the sons of former leader and drug trafficker Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán. Claudia Sheinbaum herself said that the authenticity of the videos must be confirmed. Despite this caution, the videos raised a major question in Latin America: How was it possible that alleged members of some of the world’s most dangerous drug cartels were fighting in the ranks of the Ukrainian Army? These concerns come on top of the investigations that Sheinbaum’s Mexican government has launched regarding the use in Mexico of military technology similar to that used in the Russian-Ukrainian conflict. According to a theory reported by some media outlets and Mexican authorities, there is a possibility that several cartel members have infiltrated Ukrainian ranks to learn how to operate kamikaze-style drones. Foreign fighters fill Ukraine military shortages It is no secret that thousands of foreign soldiers have participated in the Russian-Ukrainian conflict, many of whom belong to mercenary groups and are former criminals, such as those operating within the group known as the Ukrainian Foreign Legion, although the full extent of how these recruitment networks operate has not yet been revealed. “Ukraine faces a severe shortage of military personnel on the front lines, and foreign fighters serve as a safety valve to avoid overburdening its own population. This creates a tension between keeping recruitment channels open and vetting applicants. Although Ukraine has collaborated with Mexico and Colombia to identify criminal actors, the screening processes remain inadequate,” Henry Ziemmer, a research associate with the Program on the Americas at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told El País . Regarding the possibility that members of Mexican drug cartels are participating in the war in Ukraine, Zimmer stated : “There are several people traveling to Ukraine with the intention of acquiring skills to bring back home, or who are already serving there and are being explicitly contacted by criminal groups. It is becoming an increasingly institutionalized method for the proliferation of drone expertise in the Americas.” Russia accuses Kyiv of training Mexican cartels For its part, the Russian Foreign Ministry alleged that nearly a hundred members of Mexican cartels have fought in the Ukrainian ranks and have been trained and educated in the use of military technology. Furthermore, it reported that the Zelenskyy government is aware of this situation. Citing an alleged US investigation into the situation in Ukraine, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s statement asserts : “The Americans have revealed that criminal groups have long been sending their militants to Ukraine to train them in the assembly and combat use of unmanned aerial vehicles.” An investigation by The Intelligence reported that while the drone academy affiliated with the Ukrainian Foreign Legion initially reserved its courses for Ukrainian nationals, it has gradually opened up its training on drone use to foreign volunteers, among whom there are a large number of Mexicans and Ukrainians. If these allegations are confirmed, Latin American governments – which have declared drug trafficking groups to be their number one enemy – would have to face even more extreme threats, specifically involving the use of advanced weapons, which some Latin American armies may not be prepared to confront. Hence, the war demonstrates once again that the spoils it leaves behind do not lie quietly on the battlefield, but are scattered throughout the world.

articles.title: Gaza faces an uncertain future a year into the ‘ceasefire’
articles.author: Ruwaida Amer
articles.content: Two million people in the Gaza Strip have been forced by the Israeli military into an area covering approximately 30% of the territory. Now, with the onset of winter, Gazan families are not only facing constant displacement, but are facing flooding in their tents. The “yellow zone” began to emerge gradually alongside the presence of the Israeli military. It encompasses areas near the Gaza-Israel border, stretching along the entire frontier from the north of the Gaza Strip to the south. As the war continued persisting into October 2025 this zone expanded significantly. It now includes the entirety of Rafah, two-thirds of Khan Yunis in the southern Gaza Strip, as well as the eastern districts of cities in the central Gaza Strip and the eastern parts of the territory as a whole. Following the announcement of a ceasefire, the Israeli military has gradually extended its reach within this zone, placing yellow concrete blocks in areas adjacent to the “yellow line” and compelling residents to displace toward the western, coastal regions. Despite it being a temporary ceasefire arrangement, the Israeli army has continued to shift concrete blocks and gradually push the “yellow line” westward toward populated areas (such as the Shuja’iyya, Tuffah, and Zeitoun neighborhoods, and the Maghazi refugee camp). Human rights organizations estimate that the area now under Israeli military control or restricted behind this line exceeds 70% of the Gaza Strip’s total territory. Palestinians are prohibited from crossing this line or returning to their homes and agricultural lands located to its east; anyone who approaches it risks being directly targeted. This has led to repeated and ongoing waves of displacement for families, as well as a severe reduction in the space available for them to live. Expanding the “Yellow Line” This area was not as extensive when the ceasefire took effect in October of last year. Over the past year, however, various parts of the Gaza Strip specifically in the east have been gradually seized, expanding the “yellow line” under Israeli military control. Under the cover of night, the Israeli military places massive yellow concrete blocks; residents wake up to find these barriers in their neighborhoods, forcing them to search for yet another place to seek refuge. Recently, the military placed these blocks in the Al-Masdar area, east of Deir al-Balah in the central Gaza Strip. Salem Al-Masdar, 45, a resident of the area, recounts: “A few days ago, the Israeli military advanced near our neighborhood. We heard the sounds of tanks and military vehicles, but we assumed it was a temporary operation that they were searching for something. It was a harrowing night for everyone; we lived through moments of sheer terror, as if the war were still raging. We waited for the military to withdraw and for the sun to rise so we could see what they had done. We didn’t dare leave our homes for fear of being shot. The next day, I heard neighbors screaming and went out to see what was happening. We discovered a yellow concrete block in the area, a sign that our lives were now in danger, as the Israeli military had brought this territory under its control.” Salem could not articulate the shock he felt at having to search for a place to take refuge within an extremely cramped area, already packed with hundreds of thousands of displaced people. He viewed this as an injustice to be forced into such a situation even during a ceasefire, a time when their lives ought to be safe and free from the need for displacement. Indiscriminate gunfire from within the “Yellow Line” Fleeing the “Yellow Line” and its surrounding areas does not spare civilians from death. On the contrary, there is daily, indiscriminate gunfire originating from the “Yellow Line” zone, directed toward the tents and areas where civilians have sought shelter. Every day, people are reported wounded by these rounds, fired from Israeli military vehicles stationed along the “Yellow Line.” Rima Harb, 35, from the Al-Mawasi area, says: “Every day, we hear the sound of tank shells and gunfire echoing through the air. A few days ago, a child from the camp was wounded while on his way to school. I am terrified for my children whenever they head to school; I make sure to accompany them. We live in fear of this indiscriminate gunfire; we never feel safe. Any one of us could be hit at any moment. It feels as though the army is everywhere, not just along the ‘Yellow Line,’ and the shelling continues unabated. We cannot walk the streets safely. Since the ceasefire began, we have never truly escaped the effects of the war; it is as if the conflict is still ongoing.” She adds: “I constantly worry about my children what if one of them goes outside and gets struck by a bullet? I live in fear of hearing one of them scream; I find myself running toward any sound I hear in the camp. I am in a state of perpetual anxiety for their lives. I try not to dwell on such a possibility, yet I keep following the news, hoping that this suffering in Gaza might finally come to an end. Our lives remain under threat in every conceivable way. It is deeply distressing that the Al-Mawasi area in Khan Yunis is so overcrowded, especially with the persistent displacement orders issued as the ‘yellow zone’ expands. We simply want our children to live in safety.” The “Green City” in Rafah – inside the “Yellow Zone “ Reports are circulating attributed to the Israeli military that there is a plan to begin constructing a “city” intended for the relocation of civilians. For the residents of Rafah who were forced to flee their city, which now falls within the restricted “yellow zone,” this news offers a glimmer of hope. Aya Abu Al-Rous, a 38-year-old mother of three from Rafah, was forced to flee her home for the Al-Mawasi area. She describes her daily existence as a living hell, stating: “I have never been able to accept living in a tent, not even for a single day. I have been displaced here for three years, yet I still haven’t adapted. This life bears no resemblance to the life I once knew. I want to return to Rafah as soon as possible; I would be the first to agree to go back, under any circumstances even if it meant living under the control of the Israeli military. This tent has stripped me of any privacy with my family. I cannot sleep, nor can I properly care for my children. It is freezing cold in the winter and sweltering, unbearable, in the summer. Every single day, I weep over the loss of my home and my city.” She adds: “I have often wished that I had never left my home. I imagine myself back on the city streets; I long to take my children to their schools. Now, we are forbidden from returning, as those areas fall within the ‘yellow line’ a zone that cannot be crossed. We hear the sound of stray gunfire from Israeli tanks and snipers, which fills us with immense fear. My only desire is to keep my children safe until we can return to the city of Rafah. From the images we see, it has been reduced to total ruin, yet I still want to go back even if it means setting up a tent amidst the rubble. I cannot breathe here; I miss my city so deeply. This is a sentiment shared by all its residents, whose lives were upended by forced displacement.” Two million Gazans are suffering because of the shifting “yellow line,” which poses a constant threat to their lives even when they are at a distance from it. This nightmare did not end with a ceasefire; rather, it has only worsened as the “yellow zone” expands and concrete barriers are shifted. Palestinians wait for the moment this nightmare will finally end, yet they have no idea when that might be.
